title: Signature Five-Minute Notice Reader
body:
The Signature Five-Minute Notice Reader is Manon's original design for a reading method that finds five answers before any sign-up: what is collected, why, who else receives it, how long it is kept, and how to contact the service. Its premise is that nobody reads every notice, so a method that takes five minutes and is actually used beats a perfect method that is never used.

The design treats a notice as a document with a shape, and teaches readers to read the shape, not every word.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature five-minute notice reading. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Scan headings for the five answers first
  2. Note collection beyond what the service needs
  3. Note sharing recipients and purposes
  4. Note retention and deletion routes
  5. Decide on the five answers before signing up

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Five answers found; OK :: Excess collection noted; OK :: Sharing noted; OK :: Retention and deletion noted; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The reader is a screening method, not legal analysis, and it cannot interpret any notice's legal meaning. Where sensitive or children's data is governed, a fuller reading or professional advice is warranted. A common mistake is accepting unread because the notice is long, which is what its length is designed to encourage. title: Signature Browser Privacy Dial
body:
The Signature Browser Privacy Dial is Manon's original design for a dial with deliberate positions: cookie handling, tracking protection, site permissions, and clearing on exit, each set consciously rather than left at defaults. Its premise is that a browser's defaults are someone else's choices, and a dial turned deliberately replaces them with the user's own.

The design exists because defaults are decisions made for you, and a dial is how you make them yourself.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature browser privacy dial. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Read each privacy section before changing anything
  2. Set cookie handling to the strictest comfortable level
  3. Turn on tracking protection where offered
  4. Review site permissions for location, camera, microphone, and notifications
  5. Set clearing on exit where it fits your use

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Sections read; OK :: Cookie handling set deliberately; OK :: Tracking protection on; OK :: Permissions reviewed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The dial is a review habit, not a feature of any particular browser, and stricter positions can break sites, which then need per-site exceptions. Its honesty is that it promises deliberation, not invisibility. A common mistake is changing one switch and assuming the browser is private. title: Signature Cookie Choice Card
body:
The Signature Cookie Choice Card is Manon's original design for a card kept by the screen: on every banner, choose reject or manage, never accept-all by reflex. The card explains why in one line: accept-all is the broadest permission, granted to dismiss an annoyance. Its premise is that a habit needs a reminder at the moment of action, not a lesson remembered from last month.

The design puts the reminder where the click happens, because that is where habits are made.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature cookie-choice card. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Choose reject or manage, never accept-all by reflex
  2. Allow necessary cookies and refuse tracking cookies where offered
  3. Clear cookies periodically
  4. Block third-party cookies in browser settings where offered
  5. Revisit choices after site redesigns

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Reject or manage chosen; OK :: Necessary allowed, tracking refused; OK :: Cookies cleared periodically; OK :: Third-party cookies blocked; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The card is a habit aid, not a legal reading of any banner, and some sites limit features when tracking is refused. Its value is the reflex it builds: pause, choose, continue. A common mistake is clicking accept-all to dismiss the banner. title: Signature Location Ledger
body:
The Signature Location Ledger is Manon's original design for a ledger of location grants: each app, its setting, and the reason it was granted, reviewed monthly. Its premise is that location is a diary written without words, and a ledger is how a diary's readers are chosen deliberately rather than by default.

The design treats location grants as loans of a diary, and loans as things that need a list.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature location-permission ledger. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List every app with location permission
  2. Set most to never and a few to only while in use
  3. Justify each always grant individually, or remove it
  4. Remove location from shared photos where offered
  5. Review the ledger after installing new apps

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Location apps listed; OK :: Most set to never; OK :: Always grants justified; OK :: Photo location removed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The ledger is a personal record, not a system control, and some apps genuinely need location while in use. Where an app demands always location, the ledger's answer is to weigh that cost openly. A common mistake is granting always location once and forgetting the grant forever. title: Signature App Permission Map
body:
The Signature App Permission Map is Manon's original design for a map of installed apps and their permissions, drawn by the user and tested by one question per permission: does this app's job need this. Its premise is that permissions are forgotten because they are scattered, and a map makes the scattered visible and therefore removable.

The design exists because a permission nobody can find again is a permission nobody will ever remove.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature app-permission map. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List apps and their permissions on the map
  2. Test each permission against the app's job
  3. Remove permissions that fail the job test
  4. Uninstall unused apps
  5. Redraw the map after major updates

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Apps and permissions mapped; OK :: Job test applied; OK :: Failing permissions removed; OK :: Unused apps uninstalled; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The map is a personal record, not a reading of any system's controls, which differ between systems. It does not cover system permissions that cannot be changed. A common mistake is granting every permission at install to reach the app faster. title: Signature Ad Switchboard
body:
The Signature Ad Switchboard is Manon's original design for a board with three switches: device, browser, and ad accounts actually used, each set deliberately and recorded. Its premise is that ad controls are scattered across settings, and a switchboard gathers them where they can be set together and reviewed together.

The design gathers scattered switches, because scattered switches are switches nobody sets.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature ad-personalization switchboard. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Set the device ad switch deliberately
  2. Set the browser ad switch deliberately
  3. Set ad switches in accounts actually used
  4. Record the settings and expect general ads, not no ads
  5. Review the board after device or account changes

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Device switch set; OK :: Browser switch set; OK :: Account switches set; OK :: General ads expected; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The switchboard is a review habit, not a promise of ad-free browsing, since some tailored advertising continues through channels these switches do not govern. Its honesty is its strength: it promises a change in basis, not an end to ads. A common mistake is believing that switching off personalization removes advertising. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Signature Tracker Screen
body:
The Signature Tracker Screen is Manon's original design for a screen placed between the reader and cross-site trackers: blocking tools, private browsing for sensitive sessions, and per-site exceptions only, never global ones. Its premise is that blocking is a screen, not a wall: it reduces tracking visibly, but a site still sees its own visit, and claiming more would be dishonest.

The design promises less tracking, not no tracking, because honesty is what makes a screen trustworthy.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature tracker-blocking screen. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Use blocking for known trackers
  2. Use private browsing for sessions that should not persist
  3. Prefer search tools that do not profile queries
  4. Allow broken sites only per-site, never globally
  5. Combine blocking with cookie and permission habits

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Blocking in use; OK :: Private browsing for sensitive sessions; OK :: Per-site exceptions only; OK :: Combined with cookie habits; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The screen is a habit combining tools, not a recommendation of any particular tool, whose blocking and funding differ. Its combination rule is the protection: no single tool suffices alone. A common mistake is installing a blocker and assuming invisibility. title: Signature Fingerprint Fog
body:
The Signature Fingerprint Fog is Manon's original design for fog around a browser's fingerprint: standardizing details where possible, avoiding unusual additions that increase uniqueness, and never mistaking cookie clearing for full privacy. Its premise is that a fingerprint is a face made of small details, and fog does not erase the face, but makes it harder to recognize at a distance.

The design is honest about partial defenses, because a partial defense presented as total is a trap.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature fingerprint-limiting fog. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Learn what fingerprint details are collected
  2. Understand cookie clearing does not defeat fingerprinting
  3. Use a browser that standardizes details where possible
  4. Avoid unusual fonts and extensions that increase uniqueness
  5. Combine fog with other habits, never alone

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Fingerprint concept learned; OK :: Cookie myth rejected; OK :: Standardizing browser used; OK :: Uniqueness additions avoided; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The fog is a concept and a set of habits, not a guarantee of unrecognizability, since fingerprinting defenses are an arms race. It does not cover fingerprinting for security purposes, which is a different use of similar techniques. A common mistake is believing cookie clearing makes a browser unrecognizable. title: Signature My-Data Letter
body:
The Signature My-Data Letter is Manon's original design for a short letter that asks a service to show the data it holds: who you are, what you ask for, how you wish to receive it, and proof of identity limited to what is required. Its premise is that a scoped letter is answered, while a vague demand for everything is delayed, so the letter's brevity is its power.

The design treats clarity as courtesy and as strategy: a reviewer can act on a clear letter without further correspondence.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature data-access letter. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Find the service's request contact or form
  2. Write a scoped request: identity, scope, format
  3. Attach only required proof of identity
  4. Keep a copy and the date sent
  5. Diary a follow-up and escalate politely if needed

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Contact found; OK :: Scoped letter written; OK :: Proof limited to required; OK :: Copy and date kept; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The letter is a drafting design, not legal advice, since access rights and deadlines vary by jurisdiction and service. Its strength is record-keeping: copy, date, and follow-up. title: Signature Correction Letter
body:
The Signature Correction Letter is Manon's original design for a letter that fixes wrong data in one pass: what is wrong, what is correct, and what evidence proves it. Its premise is that a reviewer can change a stated value with stated evidence, but cannot act on a general complaint, so the letter's precision is what makes correction possible.

The design exists because wrong data harms quietly, through decisions made on it that the person never sees.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature data-correction letter. Follow these steps in order:

  1. State the wrong value and the correct value precisely
  2. Gather supporting evidence
  3. Write a short letter: error, correction, evidence
  4. Keep a copy, the evidence, and the date
  5. Diary a follow-up and keep the reply with the request

title: Signature Erasure Letter
body:
The Signature Erasure Letter is Manon's original design for a letter that asks for deletion with its eyes open: which data or account, what will be lost, and confirmation that export happened first. Its premise is that deletion locks a door behind you, so the letter is written only after the export, and its confirmation is kept as proof of the request.

The design treats erasure as a door, and insists the export walk through it first.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature data-erasure letter. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Decide precisely what is to be erased
  2. Export what is to be kept before requesting
  3. Send through the service's published channel
  4. State understanding of what will be lost
  5. Keep the request and the confirmation

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Scope decided; OK :: Export completed first; OK :: Published channel used; OK :: Confirmation kept; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The letter is a drafting design, not a promise of complete erasure, since deletion rights have exceptions and backups cycle on their own calendar. A later design covers backups and copies, the honest limit of any erasure. A common mistake is requesting deletion before exporting, then discovering the only copy is gone. title: Signature Copies-and-Backups Tracker
body:
The Signature Copies-and-Backups Tracker is Manon's original design for tracking a deletion across every copy: live systems, backups, logs, and processors, each with its own confirmation and its own calendar. Its premise is that live deletion is instant while backup deletion is a calendar, and a tracker that separates the two prevents false confidence.

The design exists because a live confirmation is not a backup confirmation, and confusing them is the central deletion mistake.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature deletion-across-copies tracker. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Ask which systems hold copies
  2. Ask when backups cycle and data ages out
  3. Request live and backup confirmations separately
  4. Diary a follow-up after the stated cycle
  5. Keep answers with the original request

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Copy systems asked; OK :: Backup cycle asked; OK :: Confirmations separated; OK :: Follow-up diarized; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The tracker is a questioning and follow-up design, not an override of any service's lawful retention or any processor's terms. Its value is verifiability: deletion becomes something checked, not merely promised. A common mistake is accepting a live confirmation as proof that every backup is gone. title: Signature Data Carry Case
body:
The Signature Data Carry Case is Manon's original design for carrying data between services: find the export, download it, open it and check it, store it safely, and only then import or close the old account. Its premise is that data you cannot take with you is data you are renting, and a carry case is how rented data becomes carried data.

The design treats the export check as the essential step, because an unopened export is a promise, not a possession.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature data-portability carry case. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Find the export tool and format
  2. Download and store the export safely
  3. Open and check the export's contents
  4. Import elsewhere or keep it as an archive
  5. Report a failed export before closing the old account

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Export tool found; OK :: Export stored safely; OK :: Export opened and checked; OK :: Failure reported before closing; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The carry case is a habit, not a legal claim, since portability rights and formats vary and some data may not be portable. Its strength is the check: open, verify, then close. A common mistake is closing the old account before checking the export opens and is complete. title: Signature Objection Card
body:
The Signature Objection Card is Manon's original design for a card recording an objection: which use, when objected, what confirmation arrived, and whether the use stopped within the stated period. Its premise is that an objection without a kept confirmation is a claim without evidence, and the card is the evidence.

The design treats the confirmation as the objection's proof, because marketing that continues must be answered with dates, not with memory.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature objection-to-processing card. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Find the objection or opt-out control
  2. Use it and note the date and effect period
  3. Keep the confirmation
  4. Check whether the use stops in time
  5. Follow up with confirmation and dates if it does not

Use and limits. The card is a record-keeping design, not legal advice, since objection rights vary and some processing may lawfully continue. Its value is the paper trail for any follow-up. title: Signature Consent Logbook
body:
The Signature Consent Logbook is Manon's original design for a single book, paper or file, recording every permission: service, data, date, purpose, and withdrawal with its confirmation. Its premise is that a permission nobody wrote down is a permission nobody will remember to withdraw, and a logbook turns vague oversharing into a prunable list.

The design exists because memory is the weakest record-keeping system, and permissions deserve better than memory.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature personal consent logbook. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Record each consent: service, data, date, purpose
  2. Record each withdrawal with date and confirmation
  3. Keep the logbook in one place
  4. Review quarterly and prune stale consents
  5. Use the logbook to draft data requests

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Consents recorded fully; OK :: Withdrawals recorded; OK :: Logbook in one place; OK :: Quarterly review done; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The logbook is a personal record, not a legal instrument, and it does not override a service's records. It does not cover consent given on behalf of others, which needs its own care. A common mistake is keeping consents scattered across emails and messages, which is no log at all. title: Signature Quarterly Privacy Wheel
body:
The Signature Quarterly Privacy Wheel is Manon's original design for a wheel that turns four times a year: browser, apps, location, cookies, ads, trackers, consent log, and pending requests, each a spoke checked in one sitting, ending with the next wheel date set. Its premise is that privacy decays by drift, and only a scheduled wheel notices drift.

The design gives the audit a wheel and a date, because audits without a date are intentions, not events.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: control must be visible, so a setting that cannot be found does not count as a choice; control must be reversible, so trying a stricter setting never traps the user; and the user's own log is the proof, so every request, choice, and change is recorded by the user, not only by the service.

The working method is Signature quarterly privacy wheel. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Walk browser, app, and location spokes
  2. Review cookies, ads, and trackers
  3. Prune the consent logbook
  4. Check pending requests and follow-up dates
  5. Set the next wheel date before finishing

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Browser, app, location walked; OK :: Cookies, ads, trackers reviewed; OK :: Logbook pruned; OK :: Next wheel date set; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The wheel is a snapshot, and a permission granted the week after escapes notice until the next turn. The design therefore pairs the quarterly wheel with permission reviews whenever a new app is installed. A common mistake is auditing only the browser and calling privacy done.
